questions.question_text:
A male weighing $80\text{ kg}$ drinks $5$ standard drinks over $2\text{ hours}$.
Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$ to calculate his estimated BAC, correct to 3 decimal places.

options.why: Used the female formula constant of $5.5$ instead of $6.8$.
Omitted the metabolism term $7.5H$ from the numerator.
Subtracted $7.5$ only once instead of multiplying by $2\text{ hours}$.

questions.question_text:
A female weighing $52\text{ kg}$ consumes $3$ standard drinks over $2.5\text{ hours}$.
Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{female}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{5.5M}$ to calculate her estimated BAC to 3 decimal places.

options.why: Used the male formula constant of $6.8$ instead of $5.5$.
Omitted the metabolism term $7.5H$ from the numerator.
Subtracted $5.5H$ instead of $7.5H$ in the numerator.

questions.question_text:
A $75\text{ kg}$ male is at an event for $4\text{ hours}$.
What is the maximum number of standard drinks $N$ he can consume to maintain an estimated BAC at or below $0.05$?
Round to 2 decimal places.

options.why: Used the female formula constant of $5.5$ instead of $6.8$.
Forgot to add the $30$ grams from alcohol metabolism to the total.
Subtracted the metabolism term instead of adding it when solving.

questions.question_text:
A $60\text{ kg}$ woman is drinking over a period of $3.5\text{ hours}$.
What is the maximum whole number of standard drinks she can consume to keep her estimated BAC strictly below $0.05$?

options.why: Rounded up to $5$, which would give a BAC of $\approx 0.072$, exceeding the legal limit.
Used $H = 2$ instead of $3.5$, giving a boundary of $N = 3.15$, then rounded down.
Added the metabolism term twice when solving, giving $N = (16.5 + 2(26.25))/10 = 6.9$, then rounded down.
